name: Minot's Ledge
note: One flash, four, then three. Since 1 May 1894 the light has flashed this group, and because "I love you" has one, four and three letters, the tower is known locally as the "I love you" light. Count the dark between groups: it is what separates 1, 4 and 3 from a run of eight.

name: Cape Hatteras
note: A one-second flash and a six-and-a-half-second eclipse: 7.5 s in all. The flash count tells you nothing here, so the period has to: time two flashes, not one.

name: Portland Head
note: The same grammar as Hatteras, a single white flash, but nearly twice as fast. Side by side, the two lights differ only in their period.

name: Fastnet
place: Fastnet Rock, off County Cork, Ireland
note: Another single white flash, at five seconds. Three lights in a row with the same letters show why the number after them matters most.

name: Bishop Rock
note: Two flashes close together, then a long dark. A group is read as one word: the pair belongs together because the gap inside it is much shorter than the gap after it.

name: Eddystone
note: Two lights on one tower. The main light flashes white in pairs; a lower window shows a red isophase light toward the Hand Deeps, a hazard to the west-northwest. See the red and you are in the arc that covers the danger.

name: Cape Byron
place: Byron Bay, New South Wales, Australia
note: A slow white flash high on the headland, and a fixed red light seven metres below it with a far shorter charted range: 27 nautical miles for the white, 8 for the red.

name: Sandy Hook
note: A fixed light: no rhythm at all. A steady light says nothing distinctive about itself, which is why the IALA buoyage system does not use fixed lights on its marks.

name: Highland
place: North Truro, Cape Cod, Massachusetts, USA
note: Once one steady light on one tower, told from Chatham by its two towers and from Nauset by its three: you counted points of light along the horizon. Its single flash now says the one the tower used to. On the outer arm of the Cape its period is what sets it apart: 5 s, where Race Point, the only other single white flash there, takes 10.

name: Chatham
note: Lit in 1808 with two towers, where Truro had one. In 1923 the northern tower was taken down and moved about twelve miles north, where it became Nauset Light. The station still says two, now in time: the only group flash on the outer arm of the Cape.

name: Nauset
note: The tower that stood at Chatham until 1923. It flashed three times in white, the count once spelled out by the three towers of the Three Sisters of Nauset, until 1981, when rotating aerobeacons gave it one white flash and one red. The colours are charted to different ranges, so between 20 and 24 miles out the red is gone and it shows one white flash every ten seconds.

name: Race Point
note: First lit on 5 November 1816 with one of the earliest revolving lights, which set it apart from Highland's steady one. When it failed to revolve in thick weather, vessels took it for Highland: three in the winter of 1842, the schooner Saluda in 1845. Today it flashes once every ten seconds, Highland every five.

sources.title: A false beacon at Race Point Light

name: Wood End
note: Near the tip of the hook, close to Race Point and at the same rhythm: one flash every ten seconds. A stopwatch reads the same at both. Only the colour separates them, red here and white there.

name: Long Point
note: At the very end of the hook, and different from its five neighbours in everything: green, short-period, and occulting, the only one of the six lit for longer than it is dark.
